---
title: "The ash dieback model"
author: "Simon Frost"
engine: julia
---

## Overview

Ash dieback, caused by the invasive fungus *Hymenoscyphus fraxineus* ("Chalara"), reached
north-eastern France around 2008 and spread across the country in a decade.
Fritsch, Grosdidier, Gégout-Petit and Marçais built a mechanistic-statistical model of
that spread and fitted it to the national forest health survey. This vignette loads the
data, simulates the model at one parameter set, maps it, and checks the likelihood against
the authors' code, PEOC.

## Setup

```{julia}
using AshDieback
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## The data

`load_peoc_data` reads the files shipped with PEOC 1.0 and puts them on the grid of
16 km quadrats: 62 × 61 for mainland France plus three empty border quadrats on each side.

```{julia}
data = load_peoc_data()
```

The survey visits plots of about 30 trees and records the proportion with symptoms.
Repeat visits to a quadrat in a year are merged:

```{julia}
[(o.year, length(o), sum(o.visits), round(mean(o.proportion); digits = 3))
 for o in data.observations]
```

Ash density, from the national forest inventory, sets where the fungus can multiply:

```{julia}
d = copy(data.ash_density)
d[d .== 0] .= NaN
heatmap(permutedims(d); aspect_ratio = :equal, title = "ash basal area (m²/ha)",
        xlabel = "x quadrat", ylabel = "y quadrat")
```

## Simulating the epidemic

The parameter set below is close to the paper's reduced model (no Allee effect, no rainfall
effect, persistent symptoms).

```{julia}
θ = AshDiebackParameters(; r_symp = 1000.0, r_allee = 0.0, beta_0 = 30.0, beta_1 = 0.0,
                         D = 20.0, S_sat = 90.0, gamma = 22.0, C_pers = 1.0,
                         C_init = 0.0085, kappa = 0.1)
prob = AshDiebackProblem(data, θ)
sol = solve(prob)
size(sol.symptoms)
```

`sol.fungi` holds the colonised rachis per ash for 2007–2018 (the first two years imputed
from prevalence maps) and `sol.symptoms` the probability that a tree has symptoms in each
survey year 2008–2019. Plotting a solution maps one year:

```{julia}
plot(plot(sol; year = 2010), plot(sol; year = 2014), plot(sol; year = 2019);
     layout = (1, 3), size = (1200, 380), clims = (0, 1))
```

The epidemic front moves from the north-east towards the south-west: from the foci in
the north-east in 2010, by 2014 it covers most of the north-eastern half of the country.

## The likelihood

The likelihood treats the trees with symptoms in each visited quadrat as binomial:

```{julia}
loglikelihood(sol)
```

PEOC's own value at this parameter set, computed by PEOC 1.0 under Python 2.7, is
−25151.76613587413. `peoc_loglikelihood` also returns PEOC's zero-likelihood flag:

```{julia}
ll, zero = peoc_loglikelihood(sol)
(ll, zero, abs(ll / -25151.76613587413 - 1))
```

The agreement is to rounding error. It relies on solving the diffusion so that every
value of the spore field keeps its relative accuracy: far from the front the field is as
small as 1e-100, and the likelihood takes its logarithm. `SparseCrankNicolson`, the
default, does this with a sparse Cholesky factorisation; `DenseCrankNicolson` is PEOC's
original dense scheme, about 30 times slower:

```{julia}
@time solve(prob);
```

## Temperature

Hot summers slow symptom development through f(T) = ([1 − T/γ]₊)^κ, where T counts the
days over 28 °C in July and August:

```{julia}
T = range(0, 30; length = 200)
plot(T, [temperature_effect.(T, 22.0, κ) for κ in (0.1, 0.5, 2.0)];
     label = ["κ = 0.1" "κ = 0.5" "κ = 2"], xlabel = "days over 28 °C",
     ylabel = "f(T)", title = "temperature effect, γ = 22")
```
